I haven't seen a post on Voat about gloves, so I will give some hopefully helpful tips.

Removing gloves is a cause for many recontaminations - whether in food handling, or medical setting, or household cleanup, etc. Most people take latex/food prep gloves off like winter gloves - whatever works is fine. That is the wrong mentality for staying contamination free.

How to remove gloves without cross contamination:

Step 1: Remember that the outside layer of the glove has been exposed, and keep that layer from touching anything clean. Have an appropriate receptacle close by for glove disposal.

Step 2: Grab the exposed layer of one glove by the wrist part with the fingers of the other hand. Do not insert the fingers under the glove, use the fingers of one glove (glove A) to grasp the top side of the other glove (glove B) near the wrist, pinch and hold this glove (B) by the outer exposed layer.

Step 3: Gently (depending on the contamination, excessive movement can cause airborne contamination again) peel back the wrist part of the glove (B) to about halfway down the palm of the hand (hand B). This should expose some of the inner layer of the glove (B) - which is clean and uncontaminated and will be used later. Gently slide the fingers of glove (A) out, keeping them under the peeled back layer of glove (B) to keep the inside layers of glove (B) clean. Try not to disturb glove (B) too much with the inner layer exposed.

Step 4: With the glove that is half peeled back (glove B), use the fingers to grab the wrist part of the other glove (glove A), and slowly peel glove (A) all the way off (keeping in mind the possibility of airborne contamination) and do not let the glove (A) just swing freely after removing it, immediately put the glove (A) into the disposal container.

Step 5: With the clean fingers of the now gloveless hand (hand A), grasp the doubled over clean inner layers of the first glove (glove B), as far away from any exposed outer layers - one finger on top, and one finger inside along the palm to get a good grip, and pull the glove (glove B) off slowly, then deposit in the disposal container. Do not contact any other materials in and around the disposal container, and then seal up the container.

Step 6: Wash hands to remove any possible cross contamination and other remaining materials.

There are videos on how to remove gloves, which is good, and most of these videos put one glove in the other for easy disposal. That is a good method for containing very messy contaminations - the drawback is that without practice, the second glove hand is very prone to cross-contamination.

Sandwich shops - looking at you, Subway - fail to properly train food handlers how to do this. If they ever change gloves, watch how they do it. Usually they will use one hand to reach inside and pull the entire glove off, and then use the bare hand to remove the other glove - which cross contaminates both hands.

Then usually those same hands immediately reach for new gloves (contaminating all gloves being touched) and the process repeats.
